results.title: Gianni Infantino's alleged lover 'paid off by UEFA' as FIFA President faces growing pressure to step down
results.description: Gianni Infantino is facing growing pressure to step down after an alleged lover of the FIFA President was paid off by UEFA, which Infantino has called "categorically untrue". The Telegraph said the woman received a six-figure sum after allegedly having an affair with him while he was the European governing body's general secretary. The woman was a junior employee who received a promotion and a 30 per cent salary increase from Infantino during the period of their alleged relationship. Michel Platini, then serving as UEFA president, appeared to be made aware of the situation and raised his concerns directly with Infantino. TRENDING Stories Videos Your Say The European governing body acknowledged the arrangement in a statement, saying: "We are aware of the allegations and can confirm a departure payment was made to the individual in question, coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school. "The payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time." Infantino first joined UEFA in 2000 as a lawyer, steadily rising through the organisation before being appointed secretary general in 2009. He has been married to Leena Al Ashqar since 2001, and the couple have four daughters together. LATEST SPORTS NEWS Andrew Flintoff steps down from role as England Lions head coach England striker Ivan Toney charged with assault at Soho nightclub Newcastle admit they 'didn't want to sell Bruno Guimaraes' to Arsenal Following Sepp Blatter's downfall, Infantino won the FIFA presidency in 2016 and subsequently secured re-election in both 2019 and 2023. Prior to the current turmoil, he had been widely expected to claim a fourth term at the FIFA congress in Morocco, scheduled for March. The Telegraph also reported that complaints had been made regarding Infantino's conduct at FIFA, though the world governing body has strenuously rejected those claims. FIFA responded to the allegations, with a spokesman telling the publication: "FIFA President Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. "Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory. "No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved." The situation mounts growing pressure on the 56-year-old, following his failed sell-off plan after having to scrap a £3.1billion stake in the World Cup to private investors after it drew widespread criticism across the football world. UEFA has responded by threatening to withdraw from all FIFA tournaments for as long as Infantino remains in charge, a stance that would inflict severe commercial damage on the governing body. Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness has announced her intention to file a complaint with FIFA's Ethics Committee. Despite the mounting opposition, Infantino retains considerable backing from football federations across Africa, South America and Asia - a coalition that could prove sufficient to repel any formal leadership challenge at the March election. Following crisis talks on Wednesday, the governing body's hierarchy rallied behind Infantino, who has pledged to continue in the role despite the growing chorus calling for his departure. The FA has voiced its concerns surrounding Infantino, withdrawing its letter of support for Infantino's re-election. Our Standards: The GB News Editorial Charter

results.title: Senate Republicans narrowly confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general
results.description: WASHINGTON: US Senate Republicans on Saturday narrowly confirmed Todd Blanche to be President Donald Trump’s attorney general, capping one of the most contentious cabinet fights of Trump’s second term after bipartisan concerns over Blanche’s independence nearly derailed the nomination. Blanche won confirmation in a 50-49 vote, with Republican Senators Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski opposing him. Senator Bill Cassidy was the deciding vote after announcing Friday he thought Blanche was the best option Trump would put forward. The vote was the culmination of a weeks-long standoff between Senate Republicans and the Trump administration over Blanche, who has served as acting attorney general since April and previously ran day-to-day Justice Department operations as its second-ranking official. Republican senators had raised concerns about Blanche’s handling of the release of Jeffrey Epstein-related documents, as well as his role in establishing Trump’s $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund and a related tax-immunity agreement for Trump and his sons. Blanche confirmation vote scheduled for Tuesday after Trump says ‘weaponization’ fund is dead But Blanche overcame those challenges in frantic meetings around Capitol Hill over the last several weeks, ultimately agreeing in writing to narrow the tax-immunity agreement and end the “weaponization” payments, which critics have called a slush fund for Trump’s allies, including those who rioted at the Capitol on January 6, 2021. Both the tax-immunity agreement, which barred the IRS from auditing previous tax returns of Trump, his sons and their family business, and the fund emerged from Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. Concern over slush fund Questions remain, though, about whether that commitment is legally binding, and whether Trump, who has said he loves the idea of the fund, could later press Blanche, his former personal attorney, to revive a similar program under another name. That concern was central to the last two Republican senators Blanche needed to convince — Bill Cassidy and Lisa Murkowski — both of whom met with Blanche on Wednesday after signaling they had not yet decided how they would vote. Murkowski had cited her lack of confidence in Blanche to “check the worst impulses of this administration.” “I take issue with the handling ‌of ⁠the release of the Epstein files; the sweeping immunity protections granted to the President, his family, and their businesses; the statements that have been made to anti-abortion groups; and the repeated targeting of individuals ranging from former administration staff to sitting U.S. Senators,” Murkowski said in a post on social media platform X. Trump says he will nominate Todd Blanche as US Attorney General Cassidy, who represents Louisiana, criticized Blanche’s role in settling Trump’s IRS lawsuit but said he ultimately trusted Blanche to give the president ​candid legal advice. Blanche will take the helm of a Justice Department that has undergone significant change in the first year and a half of Trump’s second term. Under Blanche’s leadership, the department has sought prosecutions of Trump’s perceived enemies, caused the mass departures of career prosecutors and stated that it served at the direction of the president, a break with longstanding norms of independence. Crime at record lows Federal judges have on multiple occasions criticized prosecutors for bringing what they described as weak cases, and grand juries have declined to indict in some instances. Political appointees also removed senior career officials seen as resistant to the administration’s agenda, significantly reducing staff in the civil rights division, the ethics office and other divisions. Blanche has argued that he has helped bring crime to record lows and righted what he says are wrongs brought by the Biden administration against Trump and his conservative allies. Blanche’s supporters say he is committed to the Justice Department’s core mission of keeping the country safe. “Mr. Blanche is a tough, fair prosecutor dedicated to the rule of law, and his leadership instills that same zeal throughout the entire Justice Department,” Senator Chuck Grassley, the chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee who shepherded Blanche’s nomination, said on Friday. Some Republican skeptics have said Blanche, who spent nearly a decade as a career prosecutor in New York, is likely the most palatable nominee Trump could have put forward, and that in a permanent capacity, he is more likely to resist White House pressure.
